title: Mutations: When DNA Changes
hook: Every time a cell copies its DNA, tiny typos can slip in — most do nothing at all, a few cause disease, and rare ones fuel evolution.
key_points: A mutation is a change in the sequence of DNA.
Causes include copying errors, radiation, and certain chemicals.
Most mutations are neutral — they fall in unused DNA or don't change the protein.
Some are harmful, a few are beneficial, and they're the raw material of evolution.
content_html: A mutation is simply a change in the sequence of DNA — a typo in the genetic code. They sound alarming, but they're constant and mostly harmless: cells copy billions of DNA letters, and the occasional error is inevitable. The vast majority go unnoticed, a small share cause problems, and a rare few turn out to be useful.
extra_html: Mutations arise from copying mistakes during cell division and from outside agents like ultraviolet radiation or certain chemicals. As the NIH's genetics glossary notes, most are neutral: they fall in DNA that isn't used, or they change a codon in a way that still specifies the same amino acid, leaving the protein unchanged. Some mutations are harmful and underlie genetic diseases, while a rare few are beneficial. Crucially, mutations are the original source of all genetic variation — without them, natural selection would have nothing to act on, and evolution couldn't happen.

source.name: NIH National Human Genome Research Institute

flashcards.back_html: A change in the DNA sequence — anything from a single swapped base to a larger rearrangement of the genetic code.

choices.text: They fall in unused DNA or don't change the resulting protein

flashcards.explanation_html: Many mutations land in stretches of DNA that aren't used, or change a codon in a way that still codes for the same amino acid, so the protein is unaffected.

flashcards.prompt: What role do mutations play in evolution?

choices.text: They are the raw source of new genetic variation
They have no connection to evolution

flashcards.explanation_html: Mutations create new variation. Natural selection then acts on it — occasionally a mutation is beneficial and spreads through a population.
